hook

They promised the party of the century. A private island in the Bahamas. Supermodels. Private jets. Luxury villas. Gourmet food. The biggest stars in music. Thousands of people paid a fortune to be there. But when they landed, there were no villas. No stars. Just rain-soaked disaster tents, and one sad cheese sandwich that the whole world laughed at. This is the story of Fyre Festival.
billy

New York. Billy McFarland was a young entrepreneur with big dreams and an even bigger mouth. At twenty-two, he started a members-only card for rich young people, promising exclusive parties and VIP access. He loved the lifestyle. Fast cars, fancy dinners, and always the next big idea.
app

Then he teamed up with the rapper Ja Rule. Together, they built an app called Fyre, to let anyone book celebrities for their parties. To make the app famous, Billy came up with a wild plan. They would throw a music festival, on an island, so exclusive and so beautiful that everyone would be talking about it.
promo

They flew the biggest supermodels in the world to a beach in the Bahamas. Bella Hadid. Emily Ratajkowski. Hailey Baldwin. They filmed them on yachts, swimming with pigs, dancing on white sand. Then, on one single day, hundreds of influencers posted the same thing on Instagram. A simple orange square. Kendall Jenner was reportedly paid two hundred and fifty thousand dollars for one post.
tickets

It worked like magic. Tickets went from about five hundred dollars, up to twelve thousand dollars for a VIP package. People were promised luxury villas, private jet flights from Miami, chef-made meals, and a lineup with Blink one eighty two, Migos and Major Lazer. Thousands of people bought in. Everyone wanted to be there.
problems

But there was a problem. Billy had no festival. They lost their first island after breaking a promise to its owners. With only a few weeks left, they moved to a bare gravel lot on another island. No water system. No toilets. No houses. Experts told Billy it was impossible. He kept selling anyway.
money

Behind the scenes, money was running out. To keep going, Billy borrowed millions of dollars, and lied to investors about how much the company was really making. Local Bahamian workers built day and night, often without being paid. The villas were never built. Instead, they bought hundreds of disaster relief tents.
arrival

April twenty seventh, twenty seventeen. The first planes landed. Guests in their best festival outfits stepped onto buses, ready for paradise. What they found looked like a disaster zone. Wet mattresses. Piles of luggage dumped in the dark. And the headliners? Blink one eighty two had already pulled out. There was no stage.
sandwich

Then came the food. Instead of gourmet meals, guests got two slices of bread, two slices of cheese, and a sad little salad, in a foam box. One guest posted a photo of it. Within hours, the cheese sandwich went around the world. Guests rushed back to the airport, and some were stuck there for hours. The next morning, the festival was cancelled.
fall

The fallout was huge. Lawsuits poured in. Local workers and businesses were left unpaid. One Bahamian restaurant owner, Maryann Rolle, used about fifty thousand dollars of her own savings to pay her staff. In twenty eighteen, Billy pleaded guilty to fraud. And while he was out on bail, he ran another ticket scam. He was sentenced to six years in prison.
end

In twenty nineteen, two documentaries about the disaster came out, and millions watched. Billy was released in twenty twenty two. And then, believe it or not, he announced Fyre Festival Two. The man who sold paradise with an orange square showed that a perfect post can sell anything. Even a party that never existed. For more stories like this, subscribe to Rise and Ruin.
